entry.title: Rewriting the abstract of Tokenization - A Survey for Modern NLP

link.title: Rewriting the abstract of Tokenization - A Survey for Modern NLP

entry.content:
What I changed and why

The abstract is very long, which is adequate for such a comprehensive survey, though I thought it can be more concise, and highlight the extra contributions the survey has other than systemization of knowledge. Also, the abstract spends many words on sub words vs. character, and it feels that those are considerations anyone slightly familiar with the concept of tokenization will know.

Before and after

Before While modern language models take raw text as their input and produce raw text as output, they do not operate over text directly. Hidden in the very first step of language model pipelines is tokenization, where raw text is converted to a sequence of tokens which the model is designed to process. The dominant approach to tokenization is subword tokenization, which uses tokens whose granularity lies between that of characters (or bytes) and words. Subword tokenization is ubiquitous in modern natural language processing (NLP) due to its advantages: compared to word-level models, it solves the out-of-vocabulary problem while constraining the vocab ulary size, reducing the number of embedding parameters and logits needed. Compared to character-level models, it improves the inductive bias of models by packing more information into a token while producing significantly shorter sequences. While this technique is powerful, it is not without flaws. To name a few: it imposes a rigid system for how tokens are built, and one system may not generalize across languages; segmentation ambiguities create room for adversarial attacks; in multilingual settings, bal ancing the token allocation between high- and low-resource languages must be done explic itly; and the reliance on a static, pre-computed vocabulary means the tokenization process is disjoint from the model’s training, preventing true end-to-end optimization. There is substantial room for innovation in this domain, yet progress is contingent upon a clear un derstanding of existing methodologies and current bottlenecks. This survey aims to serve that purpose. We present tokenization in the context of the modern large language model (LLM) era and cover the breadth of areas that tokenization directly influences. We discuss algorithms, techniques, pitfalls, theory, and practice, along with jumping-off points for prospective re searchers and practitioners. We hope that this survey brings more attention to the field of tokenization as an area in which much progress is still to be made.
After Language models never see text. They see the output of a tokenizer: a pipeline of normalization, pretokenization, a vocabulary, and a segmentation algorithm that together decide what a model can represent. These choices underlie some of the most visible LLM failures, including brittle arithmetic and spelling, adversarial vulnerabilities, and a “token tax” that makes the same content cost more in many languages. Yet tokenization made up a small fraction of 2025 NLP and ML papers. We argue this neglect of tokenizers' research is structural: tokenizer ablations are costly and noisy at scale, perplexity is not comparable across tokenizers, and benchmarks typically freeze the tokenizer. This neglect is also visible through the confomism regarding choice of tokenizers - we complement the survey with a census of over 420k Hugging Face models and an audit of frontier tokenizers, open and closed. Together they reveal a monoculture: BPE with 100–275k vocabularies, and 94% of models reusing another model’s tokenizer exactly. We survey the field across the whole pipeline and model lifecycle: subword algorithms and pretokenization, writing systems and multilinguality, evaluation, non-canonical tokenizations, byte-level, latent and pixel-based alternatives, changing the tokenizer of a trained model, security, and theory. We hope that this survey brings more attention to the field of tokenization as an area in which much progress is still to be made. Each section closes with open questions, and we identify evaluation as the main bottleneck to progress.

The general rule

I wanted the abstract to actually hold the contribution, and aim for someone that is somewhat familiar with the topic, not to start “from scratch” - it’s redundant and doesn’t allow to say what’s importnat to the actual readers.

What I’m unsure about

  1. Maybe the new abstract is too concentrated on the “other than SoK” parts, and misses the SoK centrality of this paper.
  2. Maybe I’m “jumping” ahead too much and the original abstract is better for “beginner readers”?
  3. The strctural claim appears in the papaer but i gave it a more central posistion and maybe I’m incorrect in understanding the papaer (hard to get a full grasp on such a msiive paper).
entry.summary: A more concise and contribution centered rewrite of the abstract.

entry.title: copyedit 4.1
entry.content:
What I changed and why

I chose to rewrite the beginning of section 4.1, due to it being overly formal and complex.

Before and after

Before One common preprocessing step is to normalize the input text into a standardized form before tokenization. This may involve removing unwanted artifacts, mapping equivalent surface forms to a common representation, or applying lossy simplifications intended to reduce superficial variation in the data. Common surface-level transformations include: ... (good examples) These normalizations are often used to unify minor typographical differences across scripts for easier processing or to clean up erroneous text. Invisible character removal is also important for tokenizer safety, as control characters can be used to inject token breakpoints to alter a model’s output while leaving the surface form of the text unchanged (see also Section 14.3; Boucher et al., 2022).
After Before tokenization, text is often normalised into a standard format, Such that artifacts, escape or control characters do not exist. This is to prevent mapping of two visually similar text to different tokens and consequently different embeddings. ... (examples) Further more, control characters can be used to inject token breakpoints to alter a model’s output. Removing such "invisible characters" helps circumvent that safety risk.

The general rule

Use simple words to convey a simple idea.
entry.summary: One sentence that makes people want to click.

entry.title: <Critique / literature review / follow-ups> of
entry.content:
TLDR

SuperBPE merges words that are frequently adjacent to each other, but what about words that frequently co-occur in sentences but not necessarily adjacent? e.g. OpenAI and chatGPT: “ChatGPT is a generative AI chatbot developed by OpenAI”, “ChatGPT creator OpenAI”… I suggest a method to represent these non-adjacent co-occurrences as a single token.

background

SuperBPE (Liu et al., 2025) trains an ordinary BPE tokenizer up to a certain point (tunable as a hyperparameter), after which pretoken boundaries are removed and superword training begins. This increases average token length, boosts compression, and improves the model’s downstream performance

SPLINTER (Gazit et al., 2025) is a pretokenization strategy for languages such as Hebrew and Arabic, where morphology is encoded in root-template patterns. It rearranges text into a linear form that better represents these structures and allows more compressed and morphologically aware tokenization. Splinter rearranges words into their root followed by additional letters and the idx they should be injected at [לומד] -> [למד ו:1], this scheme allows having a single token per root and shared verb-template tokens across roots.

Follow-up

While English does not follow such nonconcatenative templates within words (English templated are concatenative, like -er -ing -ed), it does in a sense follow them within sentences, “A took B to the C”, “A talked to B online” My suggestion is thus combining the idea of super-tokens from SuperBPE with the template scheme from Splintering. This allows compressing complex relations into a single token.

The method:

After the initial whitespace-separated BPE stage, remove word boundaries like in SuperBPE. Instead of merging frequently adjacent tokens, look for high co-occuring tokens in the same sentence and merge them. At inference, per sentence, find the largest template match from the SuperBPE table, the sentence is tokenized as that template followed by other tokens, and where within the template they should be inserted: [“A talked to B online”] -> [“talked to online”, (“A”:0), (“B:3)]

entry.title: One text, many token sequences
entry.content:
The original

Section 2.2 makes the survey’s core point in prose and one equation. A language model assigns probabilities to token sequences, while detokenization is many-to-one, so the probability of a text is the sum over all of its tokenizations,

\[p(s) = \sum_{t \in T(s)} p(t),\]

yet common practice scores only the canonical one. The survey’s overview figure (Figure 1.1) draws tokenization as a single path from raw text to token IDs, so the reader has to assemble the many-to-one picture from the text and the inline “sample sentence” example, against the impression the figure gives.

The redesign

Left: the usual picture, in which text passes through a fixed tokenizer to a single token sequence. Right: the same text spelled three ways, using the example and tokenizations from Section 2.2 (▁ marks a word-initial space). The probability of the text is the sum over all of them, but in common practice only the canonical one is scored.
entry.summary: The survey's core point in one figure: a language model scores token sequences, not text, so the tokenizer is part of the model rather than a preprocessing step.

entry.title: PickyBPE - Vocabulary Trimming Reimplemented
entry.content:
What I reimplemented

I reimplemented BPE and compared it to PickyBPE - a BPE variant used for vocabulary trimming, mentioned in the survey (section 3.1.3).

PickyBPE prunes “junk” tokens during vocabulary building. Intermediate “junk” tokens are tokens that are needed only to form long token (‘entucky’ in ‘Kentucky’). PickyBPE requires the following properties in order to properly prune.

  • Intersection over Self (IoS) metric. $IoS=\frac{\text{token-pair frequency}}{\text{token frequency}}$. The closer this value is to 1 ($IoS \in [0,1]$), the more likely the token is intermediate, as it is mostly used as a step on the way to form the next merge.
  • Token removal threshold $\tau$. A threshold for IoS value for pruning tokens. Recommended as 0.9.

To summarize, PickyBPE prunes token $a$, if there exists a token $b$ such that it satisfies $\text{IoS}(a, (a, b)) = \frac{\text{freq}(a, b)}{\text{freq}(a)} \ge \tau$.

The code

def pickybpe_training(corpus, target_vocabulary_size, tau=0.9):
    pretokenized_corpus = [
        pretoken for sentence in corpus for pretoken in pretokenize(sentence)
    ]
    base_alphabet = set(c for pretoken in pretokenized_corpus for c in pretoken)
    vocab = set(base_alphabet)
    events = []
    pruned_tokens = set()  # Prevent pruned tokens from being re-added

    while len(vocab) < target_vocabulary_size:
        token_counts = collections.Counter(
            token for pretoken in pretokenized_corpus for token in pretoken
        )
        pair_counts = collections.Counter(
            (a, b)
            for pretoken in pretokenized_corpus
            for a, b in zip(pretoken, pretoken[1:])
        )
        
        # Filter out pairs that would recreate a pruned token
        valid_pairs = {
            pair: count for pair, count in pair_counts.items()
            if (pair[0] + pair[1]) not in pruned_tokens
        }
        
        if len(valid_pairs) == 0:
            break

        max_pair = max(valid_pairs, key=valid_pairs.get)
        pair_freq = valid_pairs[max_pair]
        a, b = max_pair
        new_token = a + b

        events.append(('merge', max_pair, new_token))
        vocab.add(new_token)

        # Check IoS on multi-character components
        for component in (a, b):
            if component not in base_alphabet and component in vocab:
                ios = pair_freq / token_counts[component]
                if ios >= tau:
                    vocab.remove(component)
                    pruned_tokens.add(component)  # Mark as permanently pruned
                    events.append(('remove', component))
                    print(f"--> [PickyBPE Pruned]: '{component}' (IoS = {ios:.2f}) when forming '{new_token}'")

        for pretoken in pretokenized_corpus:
            apply_merge(pretoken, max_pair)

    return list(vocab), events, list(pruned_tokens)

Full code: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1qNGiUcsvUS8OdHkb_s3epaZSdzV1w0GR?usp=sharing

Results

  Standard BPE PickyBPE ($\tau = 0.7$) PickyBPE ($\tau = 0.9$)
Final Vocab Size 150 150 150
Tokens Pruned 0 63 30

PickyBPE pruned 63 tokens running on the training data. This granted PickyBPE’s final vocabulary meaningful tokens that didn’t appear on BPE’s vocabulary. Such as ‘ different’, ‘ information’, ‘ intermediate’, ‘ organizations’, ‘ pair’, ‘ process’, ‘ redundant’, ‘ representations’, etc. See more in colab notebook.

What I learned

In this reimplementation experience I’ve achieved deeper understanding about the Byte-pair Encoding algorithm. I’ve explored PickyBPE, which improves the vocabulary by pruning “junk” tokens, thus clearing up space for longer and more meaningful tokens within the same parameter count.

I encountered several challenges during this experiment. These helped me understand that the threshold $\tau=0.9$ ensures pruning token $a$ only if it appears almost exclusively in token $b$, not the other way around. In contrast, versatile tokens that appear in multiple, distinct words (like ‘com’ may appear in ‘communication’, ‘computational’, ‘committees’, and ‘complex’), distribute their occurrences across multiple distinct tokens. Their $\text{IoS}$ per word naturally stays low ($\tau \le 0.3$), and the token ‘com’ wouldn’t get pruned.

This highlights the design trade-off behind $\tau$: setting it too low (e.g., $\tau \le 0.3$) would mistakenly prune legitimate, reusable prefixes, destroying subword sharing. At $\tau = 0.9$, PickyBPE selectively eliminates path-dependent tokens without turning the subword vocabulary into an overfitted whole-word dictionary.
entry.summary: What I reimplemented I reimplemented BPE and compared it to PickyBPE - a BPE variant used for vocabulary trimming, mentioned in the survey (section 3.1.3).

entry.title: When Two Identical-Looking Words Are Not the Same

link.title: When Two Identical-Looking Words Are Not the Same

entry.content:
Why this matters

Can you spot the difference between these two words?

pаypаl

paypal

They look identical, don’t they? But there’s a hidden difference: the second character in the second word is not the Latin letter a (U+0061). It’s the Cyrillic letter а (U+0430), used in languages such as Russian.

Although these characters look almost identical, they have different Unicode code points. To a computer, they are different characters.

This phenomenon is known as Unicode confusables: visually similar characters that have different digital identities.

It can be exploited in homograph attacks, where attackers create deceptive usernames, identifiers, or domain names that resemble legitimate ones. A person might see a familiar name without realizing that one of its characters belongs to a completely different alphabet.

But this issue is not limited to cybersecurity. It also matters for how language models process text.

The idea

What does this have to do with tokenization?

Section 14.3 of Tokenization: A Survey for Modern NLP discusses exactly this kind of character substitution.

The authors demonstrate that replacing Latin characters with visually identical Cyrillic ones can significantly change how text is tokenized.

For example, a tokenizer might represent the familiar word attack as a single token but split a visually similar version containing Cyrillic characters into several tokens.

This means that two strings that look identical to a human can produce very different representations inside a language model.

Such changes can affect model behavior and have been investigated as a source of adversarial vulnerabilities.

Can we simply normalize the text?

Section 4.1 discusses text normalization as a possible defense. However, normalization introduces a trade-off: converting different characters into a common representation can remove distinctions that matter in some contexts.

Interestingly, standard Unicode normalization does not automatically convert Cyrillic а into Latin a. Detecting visually confusable characters requires additional mechanisms.

The takeaway

What looks identical is not necessarily identical.

A tiny difference that is almost invisible to humans can matter to computers, tokenizers, and security systems.

This is a useful reminder that text has at least two different identities: how it looks and how it is encoded.

Connection to the survey: Sections 4.1 (Normalization) and 14.3 (Tokenizer Security).

Learn more

  • Unicode Security Mechanisms (UTS #39) — The Unicode standard for detecting confusable characters and addressing related security risks.
  • Unicode Normalization Forms (UAX #15) — Explains how Unicode normalization works and what distinctions it preserves.
  • Unicode Confusables — An interactive tool for exploring visually similar Unicode characters.
entry.summary: How visually identical Unicode characters can change tokenization and create security vulnerabilities.

entry.title: Beyond Fixed Tokenization: New Strategies
entry.content:
This week’s survey discusses several limitations of traditional subword tokenization, including its reliance on fixed vocabularies and segmentation rules that cannot adapt during model training, as well as challenges in generalizing across languages. It also explores alternative approaches, such as byte-level modeling, and highlights the trade-off between sequence length, model performance, and computational cost - emphasizing that fewer tokens do not necessarily mean faster or better models.

The following two papers build on these ideas: the first addresses the computational limitations of byte-level generation, while the second further investigates how tokenization choices affect model efficiency.

1. Fast Byte Latent Transformer (Kallini et al., 2026)

This paper makes byte-level language models faster at generating text by allowing them to predict multiple bytes at once, rather than generating them one by one. The survey discusses Byte Latent Transformer (BLT) as an alternative to traditional subword tokenization, but highlights the computational challenges of byte-level generation. This paper builds on BLT and proposes techniques to make generation more efficient.

2. Compute Optimal Tokenization (Limisiewicz et al., 2026)

This paper investigates how the amount of text represented by each token affects language model efficiency, showing that the optimal degree of token compression (token size) depends on the available computational budget. The survey emphasizes that shorter token sequences do not necessarily mean faster or better models. This paper investigates that trade-off and shows why choosing the right tokenization strategy matters for efficient model training.
entry.summary: Two papers extending the survey's discussion: one addressing the noted limitations of byte-level generation, and the other further exploring the claim of why fewer tokens don't necessarily mean greater efficiency.

entry.title: How language models put words back together

link.title: How language models put words back together

entry.content:
These two papers examine what happens inside the model after tokenization, i.e., how tokens become word representations. Both connect tokenization to specific computations in attention and MLP layers.

Busigin and Pinter (2026) studies how a language model combines word fragments into a representation of the whole word. They feed an already trained model a word as a single token, such as table, and record its internal representation. They then feed the same word split into fragments, such as ta | ble, and compare the representation at the final token with the original. To identify which components contribute to reconstruction, they intervene on attention and MLP outputs, replacing them with activations from other inputs and measuring how the representation changes. They find that attention brings information from earlier parts to the final token, and MLP layers help combine this information into a representation of the full word. Their main contribution is to identify the computations involved in reconstructing words after tokenization.

Kamoda et al. (2025) analyzed how attention selects which word fragments should go together. They studied GPT-2’s learned attention weights, separating contributions from token identities, positions, and their interactions. To study token identity, they fix a token such as iens and calculate its attention score against every token in the vocabulary, independently of any sentence. In one head, sap and Al receive high scores, which corresponds to words such as sapiens and Aliens. They then isolate positional contributions to determine whether the head prefers nearby tokens, and compare these predictions with attention patterns observed in real text. Their main contribution is to show that preferences for compatible subwords and nearby positions can be recovered from the model’s learned parameters.
entry.summary: Understanding how language models reconstruct words from subword tokens.

entry.title: Making the parameter cost of tokenization visible

link.title: Making the parameter cost of tokenization visible

entry.content:
The original

Table 2.1 of Tokenization: A Survey for Modern NLP supports a point made in Section 2.2: the vocabulary can account for a large share of a model’s parameter budget, especially in smaller models. The table lists vocabulary sizes, hidden dimensions, parameter counts, and embedding percentages for fifteen models, grouped by family.

The percentage column contains the comparison we need, but the reader has to assemble the picture: scan fifteen rows, mentally rank the percentages, remember the gaps, and look back at model sizes to interpret them. Every entry has the same visual weight, whether it represents almost 60% of a model or less than 1%.

The redesign replaces the table with a graph that makes these differences visible directly.

The redesign

I focus on one question: How much of each model’s parameter budget goes to the embedding and output layers? The bars show the paper’s reported percentages on a shared axis starting at zero, sorted from largest to smallest. Model names stay horizontal, and colors keep families recognizable after sorting.

Parentheses give total parameters in billions. † denotes tied embeddings: the input and output layers share parameters. The legend gives each family’s vocabulary size. Hover or tap a bar for its value; click a family in the legend to hide or show it. On narrow screens, scroll horizontally.

What the graph makes easier to see

  • Differences are visible at a glance. Bar lengths let readers see how much the parameter shares differ without mentally comparing a column of numbers. Sorting makes the ranking clear and helps both large gaps and small differences stand out.
  • Colors make comparisons easier. Models from the same family share a color, so readers can quickly find related models even when sorting places them apart. This makes it easier to compare models within a family and see how families compare with one another.

Design decisions

  • Sort by percentage. Readers can find the extremes and follow the ranking without constructing it themselves.
  • Focus on one metric. Leaving out hidden dimensions and absolute embedding counts allows the users to focus on what’s important.
  • Preserve family context with color. Consistent colors reconnect related models after sorting.

A smaller share in this graph means fewer parameters allocated to these layers relative to the model’s total; it does not by itself establish better model quality.

Data: Table 2.1, p. 10, shown above.
entry.summary: Replacing Table 2.1 with a ranked bar chart makes differences easier to see and model families easier to compare.
